items.title: AMD guides Q4 revenue to about $17B as data center nearly doubles to $8.5B; shares jump after hours
items.summary: AMD reported Q3 revenue of $13.4B (+45%), above the high end of its guidance, with non-GAAP EPS of $2.09. Data Center revenue was $8.5B, up 97% year over year, on record Instinct GPU and EPYC sales. It guided Q4 revenue to about $17B plus or minus 3%, with data center up about 50% sequentially as Helios racks and Venice ramp. Shares rose roughly 7-8% in extended trading.
items.why_it_matters: The Q4 guide is the clearest sign yet that Helios and MI450 are ramping at scale after a month-long chip sell-off, and it sets the bar for Nvidia's results later this month.

items.title: Florida regulators vote 5-0 to reject Duke Energy's data center tariff under the new SB 484 law
items.summary: The Florida Public Service Commission voted 5-0 on Nov 3 to reject Duke Energy Florida's proposed 50 MW large-load tariff. It found the plan failed to show compliance with SB 484, which requires large-load customers to bear their full cost of service. Staff had recommended denial with leave to refile. Tampa Electric's own large-load tariff is next in line.
items.why_it_matters: It is the first test of Florida's data-center cost-shifting law and a template for utilities elsewhere as ratepayer backlash grows.

items.title: Anthropic's FlashProve proves LLM outputs with a zkSNARK, at roughly 70-95x overhead on a 400B MoE
items.summary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team open-sourced FlashProve, which lets a verifier check that tokens came from a committed model without seeing the weights. On one H100 the prover reaches about 110 tokens/s on Llama 4 Maverick (400B MoE, 4-bit, ~17B active), roughly 72x overhead versus vLLM at a 24-request batch. Each proof is ~18.8 MB per 1,024-token window and the CPU-only verifier takes ~17-21 s. Limits: greedy decoding on an integer model, 1,024-token context. TechCrunch covered it on Nov 3.
items.why_it_matters: It is a concrete step toward verifying which model produced an output, relevant to compute monitoring and tamper detection, though still costly.

items.title: Anthropic: Claude-assisted work yields first 3D structure of a bacterial/phage vault particle in under four months
items.summary: Anthropic's life-sciences team says Claude searched about 15B predicted proteins for vault-protein relatives. Of 44 candidates tested, 15 of 24 expressed in E. coli gave soluble protein, seven formed vault-like particles and cryo-EM confirmed vault shape for four. The phage protein L05 forms a 96-copy, ~9.5 MDa vault versus 78 copies in mammalian vaults. Claude ran the cryo-EM pipeline in an internal multi-agent setup, and the post lists its errors, including a skipped step that produced a map blended with its mirror image.
items.why_it_matters: A concrete, error-disclosing example of an AI agent running a wet-lab plus cryo-EM discovery loop; it cut a 3-day purification to about 90 minutes.

learn.title: MoE: why compute follows active parameters but memory follows total
learn.why_today: FlashProve's prover cost is described as scaling with the ~17B active parameters of a 400B mixture-of-experts model.
learn.explanation: A mixture-of-experts layer routes each token to a few experts, so per-token FLOPs are about 2 times the active parameters, not the total. Every expert must still be resident in memory because any token may route to it, so weight memory scales with total parameters times bytes per weight. Hence an MoE can be cheap per token yet need a large accelerator pool or heavy quantisation to hold. The saving is not free: routing creates load imbalance and all-to-all communication, and small batches touch many experts, erasing the arithmetic advantage. The numbers below use the 400B/17B/4-bit figures from the item for illustration only; they are not measurements of any system.
learn.python:
# Illustrative MoE arithmetic (numbers from the FlashProve item; the rest is toy).
total, active = 400e9, 17e9
bytes_per_param = 0.5            # 4-bit weights
weights_gb = total * bytes_per_param / 1e9
flops_per_token = 2 * active     # ~2 FLOPs per active parameter per token
dense_flops = 2 * total
print(f"weights in memory: {weights_gb:.0f} GB (set by TOTAL params)")
print(f"compute/token: {flops_per_token/1e9:.0f} GFLOP vs dense {dense_flops/1e9:.0f} GFLOP")
print(f"MoE compute saving: {dense_flops/flops_per_token:.1f}x")
